user_turns:
I need to vent and then I need a plan. Thursday night our biggest prospect ever, a hospital network, sent a final offer: $480k a year, which roughly doubles our revenue. It lapsed at 10 the next morning and a competitor was in the final round. I called Tom twice and texted him. Nothing. He went dark the one night it mattered. Friday morning I spent two and a half hours on the phone with the hospital, got the timeline pushed from ten weeks to fourteen, and got an extension clause on top. Then I signed. We have nine months of runway. I wasn't going to let it walk.

Tom calls me at 10, says I committed his team without him, and hangs up on me. An hour and a half later he posts in the engineering channel that we "did not agree" to the timeline and tells everyone not to start. In front of the whole team. He has sandbagged most of what I've brought him this year because of his migration, which is now five months late. I think he wants the migration as his excuse to never touch the sales side. I'm exhausted from carrying this company by myself.

Our founders' meeting is Monday at 9. How do I handle Monday?

results.result:
This is a founders’ meeting with a signed deal and a public split already in the engineering channel. I’ll pull the meeting-prep guidance and any prior context on Tom and this deal before laying out Monday.The contract is signed. Monday is about unblocking delivery and setting a rule for the next lapse, not about getting Tom to admit the year.

It’s Monday afternoon. If 9am already happened, the three outcomes below are still the unfinished business today. If you meant next Monday, run the meeting this way.

## What you walk out with

Three decisions, written down before you leave:

1. **The hospital work starts.** One engineering owner, the first milestone inside the fourteen weeks, and what the extension clause is actually for.
2. **The engineering-channel note is withdrawn the same day**, in that channel, by Tom. The team heard a stop-work. Until that is reversed, they will wait to see which founder wins.
3. **A lapse rule.** When one founder is unreachable and an offer dies the same morning, the other can bind the company, then the argument stays between founders.

Skip the apology, the motive, and the year-in-review. “You are using the migration to avoid sales” ends the meeting. He will defend his character, and you will leave without an owner.

## Before you walk in

One page, times only:

- Thursday night: final offer, dead at 10am, competitor still in it.
- Two calls, one text, no reply.
- Friday: two and a half hours with the hospital, ten weeks moved to fourteen, extension clause added, then you signed.
- 10am: he called, said you committed his team, hung up.
- About 11:30: engineering channel, “we did not agree,” do not start.

Read the extension clause until you can say, in one sentence, what triggers it and what it costs if you miss fourteen weeks. That clause is your whole defense against “the timeline is fiction.” If you are fuzzy on it, he will be right that the team was committed to a number nobody can stand behind.

Write the three outcomes on a card. When the year comes up in your throat, look at the card.

## How to open

About two minutes:

“The hospital contract is signed. It doubles our revenue, and we have nine months of runway. I tried to reach you Thursday night and you were dark. I moved them from ten weeks to fourteen and added an extension before I signed. You should have been on that call. Committing the team without your yes is on me. Telling them not to start after we signed is on you. I need three decisions before we leave: work starts, the channel note comes down today, and we write the rule for the next time one of us is unreachable.”

Then stop. Ask one question and let it sit:

“If you had picked up at 9:30, what would you have done with an offer that died at 10 and a competitor still in the round?”

If he says he would have let it lapse, make him say that as the decision. The alternative to your signature was a dead offer and nine months of runway. That is the trade you refused. He can still hate the process.

## The channel post

This is the non-negotiable. Same channel, today, from him. Short:

“The hospital agreement is signed. My note not to start is withdrawn. Staffing and timeline get settled between founders, and I’ll post the plan.”

You are not negotiating that into a maybe. A founder stop-work in public is not a veto of a signed contract. If he refuses, you post the factual version yourself: the agreement is signed, work starts, founders are resolving staffing. No narrative, no screenshots, no “Tom was wrong.”

## Force the capacity trade

“The migration is five months late. This contract is fourteen weeks plus an extension. Which one moves, and to what date?”

Accept only a name and a date. “The team is busy” is not a plan. The workable version is usually: he stays on the migration, someone else owns the hospital, you review risk weekly, and the extension clause is the buffer for whatever the first milestone cannot hold. If he will not name a person, ask him to say out loud that he will not staff a signed contract. That sentence is the fact you manage the customer with. Do not threaten back.

## The rule you write in the room

If a commercial offer lapses within twenty-four hours, and the other founder has been called and texted with no reply by two hours before the deadline, the reachable founder may sign. Within an hour they send a written summary of what was promised. Objections go to the signer before any team channel. Nobody countermands a signed commitment in Slack.

## If he relitigates

Stay on the three decisions. If he says you don’t respect engineering: “I’m asking you to own the plan.” If he hides behind the migration: “Then give me the ship date and the people who are free for the hospital.” If he hangs up again, the recap still goes out in writing, and the team still gets the factual note that work starts.

After the meeting, send five lines to both of you: owner, first milestone, extension trigger, channel correction posted, lapse rule. Then a thirty-minute working session this week with the person who actually owns delivery.

Leave the exhaustion speech at the door. You already carried the deal. Monday is the staffing plan and the public correction.

You are right about the decision that mattered. You are not right about everything that happened around it.

You were right to sign. The offer died at 10, a competitor was still in the round, you called twice and texted, and you bought four extra weeks plus an extension before you committed. With nine months of runway and a deal that doubles revenue, letting it lapse so Tom could be in the room would have been the worse call.

You are right about the engineering-channel post. Disagreeing with you is allowed. Hanging up, then telling the team not to start on a signed contract, is a different act. That one has to come down.

He is also right that you committed his team without him. Two missed calls do not turn a fourteen-week hospital delivery into a decision he already made. That is a process failure, and it is yours. It does not unwind the signature.

The part to drop is the motive. A migration that is five months late, with sales work waiting behind it all year, is a fact you can put on the table. “He wants an excuse to never touch sales” is a theory. If you walk in needing him to admit that, you will lose the staffing plan while you win the argument.
